analysis.one_liner: Repeals nondiscrimination rules for employer health and life benefit plans.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors and never reached a vote; Congress later repealed the same rules in the 1989 budget law.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1986 tax law required employer health and life insurance plans to be offered broadly and equally — if a plan favored executives over rank-and-file workers, the value of benefits for highly paid employees was supposed to become taxable income. This bill would wipe out those rules and put tax law back the way it was before 1986. It never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that sponsor benefit plans, who would be spared the compliance paperwork and the pressure to extend health and life coverage to lower-paid workers. Highly compensated employees also gain, because their executive-tier benefits could no longer be taxed when plans discriminate in their favor.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the requirement that employer benefit plans meet coverage and benefit nondiscrimination tests, ending the compliance burden created by the 1986 and 1988 tax laws.
Restores prior tax law, applied as if the nondiscrimination provisions had never been enacted.

analysis.who_pays: Lower-wage workers, who lose the tax-law push that was nudging employers to extend health and life coverage beyond the executive suite, and the Treasury, which loses the revenue from taxing discriminatory executive benefits.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the nondiscrimination rules removes the main legal pressure on employers to offer health and life coverage broadly, so plans can once again be designed to favor highly compensated employees.
The bill would restore a system in which executives can receive valuable untaxed benefits while lower-paid employees at the same company get little or nothing from the same plans.
The Treasury would forgo the revenue raised when discriminatory plans make executive benefits taxable income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers had a real grievance: section 89's testing rules were notoriously complex and threatened to tax ordinary workers' benefits at companies that failed them, and many businesses argued the rules did more harm than good. But this bill would have fixed that by simply deleting the fairness requirement altogether — sparing companies the paperwork while also freeing them to keep richer plans for executives. A better-designed fix would have simplified the rules rather than removed them; by wiping out both the burden and the nondiscrimination principle, the bill's main lasting effect would run against lower-paid workers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee after its referral, drew no cosponsors, and never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Max Baucus introduced the bill on September 28, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

The bill would have repealed the nondiscrimination requirements for employee benefit coverage and benefits established by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and the Technical and Miscellaneous Revenue Act of 1988.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and highly paid employees got what they wanted anyway: later in 1989 Congress folded a repeal of section 89 into the omnibus budget law, replacing the rules rather than keeping them on the books.

for.name: Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal section 89 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it remained in committee from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic senator sponsored the bill with no cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: Repeal would have ended the testing and paperwork burden of section 89, but also the pressure to extend health and life coverage to lower-paid workers, letting companies keep executive-favoring plans tax-free.
Under the rules being repealed, executives' benefits became taxable when plans discriminated in their favor; repeal would have protected that tax advantage.
Section 89 spawned a compliance industry for testing and plan redesign; repeal would have eliminated that business, with little direct effect on workers either way.
